title_en: Lai Yunpeng v. Beijing Sitong Lifang Information Technology Co., Ltd. — dispute over service contract
keywords_en: Civil; Service Contract Dispute; First Instance; Basic People's Court; Beijing; Natural Person; Legal Person; Contract Law; Validity of Service Terms; Whether Change of Free Email Storage Capacity Constitutes Breach of Contract; Formation of Network Service Contract; Dismissal of Claims; Free Email Service; Click-to-Accept of Service Terms; Reduction of Email Storage Capacity; Contract Dispute; Service Contract; Technology Co., Ltd. Service Contract Dispute
full_text_en:
Lai Yunpeng v. Beijing Sitong Lifang Information Technology Co., Ltd.

— service contract dispute

Plaintiff: Lai Yunpeng, male, 27 years old, residing in Heping District, Tianjin.

Agent ad litem: Meng Xiansheng, lawyer of Tianjin Sifang Law Firm.

Agent ad litem: Pan Haitao, lawyer of Beijing Junyue Law Firm.

Defendant: Beijing Sitong Lifang Information Technology Co., Ltd., domiciled at Haidian District, Beijing.

Legal representative: Mao Daolin, Chairman of the Company.

Agents ad litem: Tong Mingyou and Cui Guobin, lawyers of Beijing Kangda Law Firm, Shanghai Branch.

The plaintiff, Lai Yunpeng, filed a lawsuit with the Haidian District People's Court of Beijing against the defendant, Beijing Sitong Lifang Information Technology Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Sitong Lifang Company), due to a service contract dispute.

The plaintiff alleged: On April 22, 2001, I registered as a member on "Sina.com" operated by Sitong Lifang Company through the Internet, and used the 50-megabyte "free mailbox" service provided by the website in accordance with its promise. This free mailbox was not truly free, as all emails sent and received by users carried commercial advertisements of the website. On August 2, 2001, "Sina.com" notified all users that it would reduce the capacity of the "free mailbox" from 50 megabytes to 5 megabytes as of midnight on September 16. "Sina.com", disregarding its promises and credibility, unilaterally changed the email service and reduced the capacity of the "free mailbox" without the consent of its members, constituting a breach of contract. The plaintiff requests an order that the defendant continue to fulfill its promise to provide a 50-megabyte "free mailbox" service.

The main evidence submitted by the plaintiff: 1. The webpage of the member data page at the URL http://members.sina.cn/scgi/olduser.fcg; 2. The "Sina.com Beijing Station Service Terms"; 3. The confirmation email for successful Sina membership registration addressed to <laiyunpengl@sina.com>; 4. The email with subject "Congratulations on the official activation of your Sina free email account" addressed to <laiyunpengl@sina.com>; 5. The webpage at the URL http://mail.sina.com.cn.

The defendant argued: The "Sina.com" owned by our company provides information services to users in accordance with the service terms. When users register as members on "Sina.com", the website fully displays the contents of the website's information service terms. Only after the user clicks the "I agree" button, indicating acceptance of all the terms of service, can the member registration be completed and the "free mailbox" service be used. The email information service of the "free mailbox" is completely free and does not require users to assume other obligations. Since the website's service terms clearly stipulate that "Sina.com" has the right to adjust the service contract terms when necessary, and to change and interrupt services at any time, our company's adjustment of the "free mailbox" capacity does not constitute a breach of contract. The plaintiff's claims are not accepted.

The main evidence submitted by the defendant: 1. The third step page of the "Sina.com" membership registration process; 2. The "Sina.com Beijing Station Service Terms"; 3. The "Sina.com Free Email Service Use Agreement".

The Haidian District People's Court of Beijing found upon trial:

On April 22, 2001, the plaintiff, Lai Yunpeng, applied for membership registration through the Internet on "Sina.com" operated by the defendant, Sitong Lifang Company, and chose the "free mailbox" service provided by "Sina.com" to its members. "Sina.com" promised, when providing this service, that the capacity of the "free mailbox" was 50 megabytes and no information service fee would be charged. On the same day of registration, the plaintiff, Lai Yunpeng, received an email from "Sina.com" confirming successful membership registration and the activation of the 50-megabyte "free mailbox." During the use of the "free mailbox," "Sina.com" never charged any fees for email information services. The daily information services of "Sina.com" also include a large amount of commercial information. When users browse various types of information on the website or process personal information, the relevant pages often include prompts for commercial advertising information, but whether to read the specific content of the advertisements is up to the user. On August 2 and September 13 of the same year, "Sina.com" issued notices on its webpages to all "free mailbox" users, stating that it would adjust the capacity of the "free mailbox" from September 16, providing only a 5-megabyte "free mailbox" service, still without charging fees for email information services. On September 16, "Sina.com" uniformly reduced the capacity of the "free mailbox" of member users from 50 megabytes to 5 megabytes.

Additionally, it was found that in the online membership application and registration process of "Sina.com" operated by the defendant, Sitong Lifang Company, a specific step was established to display the website's service terms to the applicant and require the applicant to confirm. The applicant must click the "I agree" identifier, indicating acceptance of the website's service terms, before proceeding with the membership registration. The "Sina.com Beijing Station Service Terms" of the defendant, Sitong Lifang Company, consisted of fifteen articles, including the identity of the owner and operator of the electronic service, introduction to the service content, changes and revisions to the service terms, responsibilities users should follow, website announcements and notifications, and disclosure obligations. Among them, the "Confirmation and Acceptance" article stipulated: "The services provided by Sina.com will be strictly implemented in accordance with its published regulations, service terms, and operating rules. Users must fully agree to all service terms and complete the registration process to become official users of Sina.com." The "Modification and Revision of Service Terms" article stipulated: "Sina.com has the right to modify the service terms when necessary. Once the Sina.com service terms change, the modified content will be prompted on important pages. If users do not agree with the modified content, they can proactively cancel the network services obtained. If users continue to enjoy the network services, they will be deemed to accept the changes in the service terms. Sina.com reserves the right to modify or interrupt services at any time, without liability to users or third parties." In addition, when using the "free mailbox," member users were required to confirm online the "Free Email Service Use Agreement" of "Sina.com," which was substantially consistent with the content of the "Sina.com Beijing Station Service Terms."

The Haidian District People's Court of Beijing held:

Article 10, paragraph 1, of the Contract Law of the People's Republic of China stipulates: "The parties may conclude a contract in written form, oral form, or other forms." Article 11 stipulates: "Written form means a form that can manifest the content in a tangible manner, such as a contract, letter, or data message (including telegram, telex, fax, electronic data interchange, and email)." "Sina.com" provides information services to members based on the commitment of the "Sina.com Beijing Station Service Terms." This service term defines the rights and obligations of the website in providing information services to users, and is essentially an information service contract in the form of electronic data text. According to the website's programming design, the specific content of the service terms is fully displayed to users on the website's pages. When applying for membership, the applicant can agree to the specific rights and obligations under the terms and proceed to the next step of the application, or can disagree and abandon the application. According to the membership application steps, the applicant can only complete the membership registration after clicking "I agree," i.e., confirming the content of the service terms. The plaintiff, Lai Yunpeng, completed his membership registration following this procedure. It should be found that during the registration process, he noticed the website's special prompts and understood the entire content of the website's service terms. His voluntary clicking of the "I agree" identifier at the time of registration was an act of confirming the content of the website's service terms, i.e., agreeing to comply with the offer to follow the service terms of the defendant, Sitong Lifang Company's "Sina.com." The information service contract relationship between the parties was established upon the completion of the registration application by the plaintiff, Lai Yunpeng. As for the "Free Email Service Use Agreement" of "Sina.com," although the plaintiff stated that he had not seen it at the time of registration, since the "Free Email Service Use Agreement" is substantially consistent with the "Sina.com Beijing Station Service Terms," it does not affect the agreement on the rights and obligations of the parties regarding the information service.

The plaintiff, Lai Yunpeng, voluntarily chose to use the "free mailbox" information service. This service is a personal web-based email information service item provided free of charge by "Sina.com" to users. Users do not need to pay any fees or assume other obligations to send or receive emails using this service, other than agreeing to comply with the website's service terms. Providing free information services to users in the form of a "free mailbox" is the right of the defendant, Sitong Lifang Company's "Sina.com," in operating its website's network information services. Since the "free mailbox" service is unilaterally and gratuitously provided by the website to users, the website, in providing this service, has the right, for the purpose of protecting its own rights and interests, to explain or reserve the manner of providing this service and to require users of the "free mailbox" to comply, and also has the right to make reasonable changes to this service according to the agreement or declaration, provided that it does not violate the mandatory provisions of the law. After the plaintiff registered and used the "free mailbox" of "Sina.com," the defendant fulfilled its promise and provided free email information services, but it cannot be concluded from this that the defendant's unilateral provision of free email information services was a legal obligation or an obligation agreed upon by both parties. As a right of the defendant, this service can be changed, provided that the change is reasonable, does not violate the prior agreement with the user, does not harm the user's paid services, does not violate mandatory legal provisions or social public interests, it should be lawful. As for the commercial information services of "Sina.com," they are provided to users together with other information services. Regardless of whether a user registers to use the "free mailbox" to process personal information after entering the website, they will browse commercial advertising information attached to the pages. Providing other commercial information services together with the relevant information services, and even attaching a certain amount of commercial information to each page, is one of the main characteristics of commercial websites. These advertisements only prompt users to browse, not requiring them to read the content or participate in the activities. "Sina.com," as a commercial website, decides how to display commercial information on its webpages based on its own business model; users have the freedom to choose whether to accept the manner in which "Sina.com" provides commercial information services. The "free mailbox" service promised by "Sina.com" to users means not charging fees for email information services. Other aspects of information services are provided by the website according to its business practices and are unrelated to the "free mailbox" service itself. According to the information service content agreed upon between "Sina.com" and the plaintiff, Lai Yunpeng, in accordance with the service terms, whether the website attaches commercial advertising information services to the user's personal information webpage does not constitute a corresponding rights-obligation relationship with the user's use of the "free mailbox" service. When providing free email services, the defendant did not deceive or conceal anything from the plaintiff, Lai Yunpeng, nor did it increase the obligations or responsibilities of the plaintiff, Lai Yunpeng, and it did not affect the validity of the contractual agreement on the rights and obligations of both parties regarding the information service. Under circumstances where it does not violate prohibitive provisions of laws or administrative regulations, the defendant, Sitong Lifang Company's "Sina.com," changed the content of the free information service in accordance with the service terms and fulfilled its notification obligation, which does not constitute a breach of contract. If the plaintiff, Lai Yunpeng, believes that the reduced capacity of the "free mailbox" of "Sina.com" makes it difficult to meet the original purpose of his registration, he may decide to stop using it on his own.

In summary, the Haidian District People's Court of Beijing rendered the following judgment on November 15, 2001: Reject the plaintiff Lai Yunpeng's claim requesting Sitong Lifang Company to continue to provide a 50-megabyte free email service.

The litigation costs of RMB 50 shall be borne by the plaintiff, Lai Yunpeng.

After the first-instance judgment was rendered, Lai Yunpeng, dissatisfied, appealed to the Beijing No. 1 Intermediate People's Court. The reasons were: The facts found in the first-instance judgment were erroneous; the "Sina.com Beijing Station Service Terms" is a standard form contract and should be invalid. The appellant requests the reversal of the original judgment and that Sitong Lifang Company restore the original 50-megabyte email capacity. Sitong Lifang Company accepted the first-instance judgment.

The Beijing No. 1 Intermediate People's Court, upon trial, confirmed the facts found in the first-instance judgment.

The Beijing No. 1 Intermediate People's Court held:

Article 39 of the Contract Law of the People's Republic of China stipulates: "Where a contract is concluded by way of standard terms, the party providing the standard terms shall determine the rights and obligations between the parties in accordance with the principle of fairness, and shall take reasonable measures to draw the other party's attention to the terms that exempt or limit its liability, and shall explain such terms upon the other party's request. Standard terms are clauses prepared in advance for repeated use by one party, which are not negotiated with the other party at the time of concluding the contract." Article 40 stipulates: "Standard terms that fall under the circumstances specified in Articles 52 and 53 of this Law, or where the party providing the standard terms exempts itself from liability, increases the liability of the other party, or excludes the main rights of the other party, shall be invalid." Article 52 stipulates: "A contract is invalid under any of the following circumstances: (1) one party concludes the contract by means of fraud or coercion, harming the interests of the State; (2) malicious collusion harms the interests of the State, the collective, or a third party; (3) using a lawful form to conceal an unlawful purpose; (4) harming the public interest; (5) violating the mandatory provisions of laws and administrative regulations." Article 53 stipulates: "The following exemption clauses in a contract are invalid: (1) those causing personal injury to the other party; (2) those causing property loss to the other party due to intentional act or gross negligence." The content of the website service terms displayed on the webpages of "Sina.com" operated by the defendant, Sitong Lifang Company, conforms to the characteristics of being prepared in advance and capable of repeated use, and thus should be classified as a standard form contract. In network information services, the website and users communicate through the network. The website's use of electronic text standard form contracts for users to choose and determine the rights and obligations of both parties regarding information services does not violate the law. Standard terms concluded by the parties shall be deemed valid as long as the agreed content does not violate the prohibitive provisions of the law. The "Sina.com Beijing Station Service Terms," as the information service contract confirmed by both parties, specifically stipulates the rights and obligations of both parties. Although these service terms are standard terms, the appellant has not demonstrated that they contain content prohibited by law, such as harming the interests of the State, the collective, or others, harming the public interest, or exempting the obligor's legal liability, increasing the obligee's liability, or excluding the obligee's main rights. The service terms shall have legally binding effect on both parties.

The "free mailbox" email service is a voluntary unilateral gratuitous service provided by "Sina.com" operated by Sitong Lifang Company. It should be determined that Sitong Lifang Company has the right to make reasonable changes to this service in accordance with the service terms. Before "Sina.com" adjusted the capacity of the "free mailbox" from the original 50 megabytes to 5 megabytes, it had previously made a statement on important pages of the website, fulfilling the notification and explanation obligations under the service terms. Its actions should be lawful and valid and do not constitute a breach of contract. The appeal request of Lai Yunpeng to reverse the original judgment and for Sitong Lifang Company to restore the original 50-megabyte email service is not supported.

Accordingly, the Beijing No. 1 Intermediate People's Court, in accordance with Article 153, paragraph 1, item (1) of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, rendered the following judgment:

Reject the appeal and affirm the original judgment.

The litigation costs of the second instance of RMB 50 shall be borne by the appellant, Lai Yunpeng.
